outcome: All-cause mortality at 28 days or in-hospital death
population: Trauma patients with significant bleeding or at risk of significant hemorrhage

hypotheses.title: Severe hypotension (SBP <70) greater mortality benefit from tranexamic acid (TXA)
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients with significant bleeding or at risk of significant hemorrhage, those presenting with initial systolic blood pressure (isbp) < 70 mmHg experience a larger reduction in 28-day / in-hospital all-cause mortality from TXA compared with patients with higher initial SBP.

subgroup.notes: Use the first recorded systolic blood pressure (pre-hospital or on-arrival, depending on dataset encoding). For CRASH_2 the timepoint should be consistent with trial baseline measurement. Expect small subgroup size in a 200-patient sample; consider pooling adjacent SBP bins for stability if event counts are very low.

rationale: Pathophysiology: Hemorrhagic shock (severe hypotension) induces tissue hypoperfusion that activates the fibrinolytic cascade (shock-induced hyperfibrinolysis). TXA is an antifibrinolytic that inhibits plasminogen activation and can reduce clot breakdown, plausibly lowering exsanguination risk in patients with pronounced shock.

Clinical trial and observational signals: Prior analyses and subgroup explorations from trauma studies (including CRASH-2 and other trauma series) have suggested greater absolute benefit of TXA among patients with more severe bleeding or physiological instability, consistent with larger untreated baseline mortality in this group.

Time-dependence synergy: Patients with severe hypotension are at high immediate risk of death from bleeding; because TXA acts early to stabilize clots, benefit is biologically plausible when administered promptly to the most hemodynamically compromised patients.

Expected absolute effect: Baseline mortality is substantially higher among SBP <70 mmHg patients, so a similar relative effect would translate into a larger absolute risk reduction and lower NNT in this subgroup compared with less hypotensive patients.
key_features: Initial systolic blood pressure (isbp) — primary effect modifier under test
Markers of shock/bleeding severity (e.g., base deficit, lactate, heart rate, need for transfusion/number of transfused units)
Time-to-treatment (delay from injury to TXA) — modifies TXA effectiveness and may interact with SBP
Injury severity (ISS or surrogate) and mechanism (penetrating vs blunt) — affect baseline risk and bleeding source
confounders_and_bias_risks: Small subgroup sample size and sparse events: with N=200 overall, the number of patients with SBP <70 (and deaths within that group) may be very small, yielding imprecise and unstable estimates and wide CIs.
Selection and measurement error in SBP: SBP may be recorded after prehospital fluids or resuscitation maneuvers, misclassifying true initial physiological state and attenuating effect estimates.

Survivor/treatment-timing bias: Patients who die very early may not receive TXA; conditioning on receipt or survival to treatment can induce bias. Time-to-treatment correlates with both SBP and outcome.

Confounding-by-indication in non-randomized settings or post-randomization selection: although CRASH-2 is randomized, subgroup discovery is data-driven and can produce chance imbalances in baseline covariates within the subgroup; residual confounding may remain if analyses are not intention-to-treat or if post-randomization variables are conditioned on.
Collider bias: Adjusting for variables influenced by both SBP and outcome (e.g., transfusion volume, operative interventions) can induce spurious associations.
Multiple testing / overfitting: Exploring many thresholds or many candidate subgroups increases type I error; apparent effect in SBP <70 may be a chance finding unless validated.

analyses: Primary test: fit an intention-to-treat Cox proportional hazards model (time-to-death up to 28 days) with terms for treatment (TXA), severe_hypotension indicator (isbp <70), and their interaction (TXA * severe_hypotension). Report interaction p-value and interaction HR with 95% CI.

Stratified estimates: estimate treatment effect within strata (isbp <70 vs ≥70) using Kaplan–Meier survival curves, log-rank test, and Cox models within each stratum to obtain hazard ratios and absolute risk differences at 28 days with 95% CIs; calculate NNT where appropriate.

Adjusted effect estimates: within each stratum, fit logistic regression (28-day mortality) or Cox models adjusting for prespecified baseline covariates (age, GCS, mechanism, ISS or surrogates, heart rate, time-to-treatment) to improve precision and reduce residual confounding; present both adjusted and unadjusted estimates.

Causal HTE estimators: apply a doubly robust estimator (e.g., targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) or augmented IPW) to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) in the SBP <70 subgroup and obtain bootstrap CIs. If feasible given sample size, use causal forest or Bayesian additive regression trees to explore continuous treatment effect modification by SBP, but interpret cautiously if events are few.

Threshold and continuous sensitivity: (a) test alternative thresholds (SBP < 60, <75, <80) to assess stability of the effect; (b) model SBP continuously with a treatment × restricted cubic spline for SBP to visualize and test continuous interaction.

Robustness / bias checks: perform per-protocol and intention-to-treat comparisons (if applicable), exclude patients receiving treatment >3 hours after injury, and adjust for time-to-treatment. Compute E-values to quantify strength of an unmeasured confounder needed to explain away observed subgroup effect.

Precision assessment: use bootstrap or exact methods to derive CIs and report event counts, and present raw 2×2 tables (dead/alive by treatment within the SBP <70 subgroup) so readers can judge stability.
negative_controls: Test whether TXA shows an effect on an outcome not plausibly influenced by antifibrinolytics (falsification outcome), e.g., early non-bleeding-related infection incidence or death from non-trauma medical causes recorded within the same follow-up window (if reliably coded).

Evaluate effect of a placebo or unrelated exposure (if available) on mortality in the SBP <70 subgroup as a falsification exposure; alternatively, test for an effect of TXA on pre-randomization variables (should be null).
robustness: Vary SBP threshold and model SBP continuously to ensure results are not threshold-dependent.
Re-run analyses excluding patients with extreme delays to treatment (>3 hours) or those who received major prehospital interventions that may alter SBP recording.
Assess balance of baseline covariates within subgroup by treatment arm; if imbalance present, present covariate-adjusted and weighted estimates (IPW using baseline covariates).
Correct for multiple comparisons or control family-wise error rate (e.g., permutation-based p-values for interaction) given exploratory subgroup discovery via HypoGeniC.
Bootstrap all CATE and interaction estimates to quantify estimation variability given small sample size.

caveats: Randomization in CRASH-2 reduces confounding for the overall treatment effect, but subgroup-specific analyses are observational comparisons within randomized arms and can be biased by chance imbalances and small numbers; a statistically significant interaction is not definitive proof of a true effect modifier without external validation.

Small sample and few events in the SBP <70 subgroup will produce imprecise estimates; wide confidence intervals and unstable point estimates are likely. Report absolute event counts and avoid overinterpretation of point estimates.
Measurement timing matters: SBP recorded after resuscitation may not reflect the pre-intervention physiological state; misclassification of isbp can attenuate or distort the apparent interaction.

Apparent greater benefit in severely hypotensive patients could reflect differential timing of care, selection of patients who survive long enough to receive TXA, or other concurrent interventions (e.g., transfusion, surgery) rather than a true pharmacologic effect of TXA specific to low SBP.

Safety considerations: TXA may alter risk of thromboembolic events; assess both benefit and harm within the subgroup. Even if mortality benefit appears greater in SBP <70, this must be balanced against potential adverse events and validated in larger datasets or pooled analyses before clinical policy changes.

Recommendation for practice change should not be based solely on an exploratory subgroup finding from a small sample. Prospective pre-specified subgroup analyses in larger trials or patient-level meta-analysis (e.g., full CRASH-2 data pooled analyses) are required to confirm effect modification.

hypotheses.title: Greater mortality benefit of TXA in hypotensive trauma patients (SBP < 90 mmHg)
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients at risk of significant hemorrhage, those who are hypotensive on presentation (systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg) will experience a larger reduction in 28-day / in-hospital all-cause mortality from tranexamic acid (TXA) compared with normotensive patients.

subgroup.split_rule: isbp < 90 mmHg defines hypotensive subgroup; compare to isbp >= 90 mmHg (normotensive/near-normal)
subgroup.notes: Use first recorded pre-randomization systolic BP (prehospital or ED triage as available). If multiple pre-randomization measurements exist, use the lowest SBP prior to TXA administration or randomization. Document measurement source (prehospital vs in-hospital). Consider sensitivity analyses using alternative cut points (e.g., 80, 100 mmHg) and continuous modelling.

rationale: Pathophysiology: Traumatic hypotension is a clinical marker of severe hemorrhage and shock, states that promote trauma-induced coagulopathy with increased fibrinolytic activity. TXA, an antifibrinolytic, stabilizes formed fibrin and reduces bleeding-related clot breakdown — mechanistically more likely to benefit patients with high fibrinolytic activation.

Clinical trial signals: CRASH-2 and other trauma studies reported larger absolute benefit of TXA in subgroups with clinically severe bleeding; these prior subgroup observations support testing increased benefit in hypotensive patients who are more likely to be severely bleeding.

Biologic plausibility linked to timing: Hypotensive patients often have active bleeding and may receive TXA earlier as an emergent intervention; since TXA effectiveness declines with treatment delay, the combination of greater fibrinolysis and potentially earlier administration increases the likelihood of a detectable treatment effect in hypotensive patients.

Predictive value of SBP: Systolic BP is an easily measured, early marker of hemodynamic compromise that is available in most trauma registries (including CRASH-2). Using SBP < 90 mmHg targets a clinically meaningful, implementable subgroup where treatment decisions are commonly considered.
key_features: isbp (first pre-randomization systolic blood pressure)
time_from_injury_to_TXA (timesensitive effect modifier)
injury_severity (e.g., ISS or proxy: GCS, mechanism, number of bleeding sites)
transfusion/early hemostatic interventions (blood product administration, surgery/intervention)
presence_of_TBI (traumatic brain injury can modify mortality causes and TXA effect)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Time-to-treatment confounding: Hypotensive patients may receive TXA earlier (or later) — time is a strong modifier of TXA effect and a potential confounder if not adjusted.

Co-interventions and care intensity: Hypotensive patients are more likely to receive urgent transfusion, surgical hemostasis, or other interventions that independently affect mortality and may interact with TXA effect.

Selection/collider bias: Restricting analysis to patients who survive long enough to receive TXA or to those with measured SBP may induce selection bias (immortal time or collider), especially in observational subsets.

Measurement error/misclassification of SBP: Prehospital vs in-hospital readings, single vs repeated measurements, cuff vs invasive monitoring differences can misclassify hypotension status and attenuate interaction estimates.

Residual confounding by injury severity or comorbidity: Even in randomized data, subgroup-specific imbalances can occur (especially in small sample, n=200), producing spurious apparent effect modification.

Competing risks and cause-of-death misclassification: All-cause mortality may dilute a bleeding-specific benefit if deaths from non-hemorrhagic causes (e.g., severe TBI, sepsis) predominate in certain subgroups.

analyses: Primary interaction test: Fit a multivariable logistic regression (or Cox proportional hazards if time-to-event available) for 28-day/in-hospital mortality with terms for treatment (TXA vs control), hypotension indicator (isbp<90), and their interaction. Adjust for pre-specified covariates: age, sex, GCS, mechanism (blunt vs penetrating), time_from_injury_to_randomization, baseline heart rate, and center if applicable. Report interaction coefficient, p-value, and 95% CI.

Estimate subgroup-specific treatment effects: Report absolute risk difference (ARR), relative risk (RR) or odds ratio (OR), and number needed to treat (NNT) with 95% CIs separately for hypotensive and non-hypotensive groups. Use bootstrap (e.g., 2000 samples) for CIs given small sample size.

Doubly-robust estimation: Use targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) or augmented IPTW to estimate marginal risk differences of TXA within each subgroup while flexibly modelling covariates (use super learner or ensemble models if feasible). Assess consistency with standard regression results.

Continuous interaction and threshold robustness: Model SBP continuously with an interaction term (TXA × SBP) using restricted cubic splines to assess whether a sharp threshold at 90 mmHg is supported, and examine other plausible cutoffs (80, 100 mmHg).

Balance and sensitivity checks: If the analysis is on a non-randomized subset or post-randomization selection, construct propensity scores for subgroup membership and/or receipt of TXA and check covariate balance within strata. Perform E-value calculation for the observed interaction to quantify the strength of unmeasured confounding needed to explain away the subgroup effect.

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses: (a) restrict to patients treated within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2 time window), (b) exclude patients with isolated severe TBI, (c) handle missing SBP via multiple imputation and compare to complete-case results, (d) exclude early deaths within 1–2 hours to assess immortal time bias.
negative_controls: Test for effect of TXA on an outcome unlikely to be affected by antifibrinolytic action (falsification), e.g., mortality due to pre-existing terminal disease or an early pre-randomization variable; alternatively, test for TXA effect on a pre-randomization baseline variable (should be null).
Compare effect estimates for causes of death unlikely related to bleeding (if cause-of-death adjudication available) to check for spurious signals.
robustness: Repeat subgroup analysis using alternative SBP definitions (lowest prehospital SBP, first ED SBP) and thresholds (80, 100 mmHg).
Use continuous modelling (splines) rather than dichotomization to avoid arbitrary cutpoint artifacts.
Perform permutation tests for the interaction term to assess whether observed heterogeneity could occur by chance given multiple hypotheses.
Assess influence of individual covariates by leave-one-covariate-out models and by calculating standardized mean differences before/after adjustment.

caveats: Sample size constraints: With n ≈ 200, subgroup analyses will be underpowered to precisely estimate interaction effects; wide confidence intervals are likely. Treat findings as exploratory/hypothesis-generating unless replicated in larger datasets.

Randomization does not guarantee unbiased subgroup estimates: Even in RCT data, randomization protects the marginal treatment effect but subgroup-specific comparisons can be imbalanced and susceptible to chance differences or post-randomization selection.

Multiplicity and statistical significance: Testing multiple potential effect modifiers increases false positive risk. Emphasize effect sizes and CIs over isolated p-values, and interpret any interaction with caution unless supported by strong prior evidence or replication.

Causality and mediation: An observed larger benefit in hypotensive patients could reflect mediation (e.g., earlier TXA administration or greater concurrent hemostatic therapy) rather than direct modification by low SBP. Distinguishing effect modification from correlated co-interventions requires careful adjustment and cannot be fully resolved in small samples.

Measurement and encoding issues: Differences in how SBP is measured (prehospital vs ED), missingness, and rounding can change classification. Document and test alternate encodings; avoid overinterpreting a single dichotomous cutpoint.

Clinical applicability: Even if an interaction is detected, operationalizing treatment decisions based solely on an SBP threshold should consider time-from-injury, risk of thrombotic complications, and totality of evidence (including larger trials and meta-analyses).

hypotheses.title: Hypertensive presentation (SBP ≥ 140 mmHg) confers no benefit and possible harm from TXA
hypotheses.hypothesis: In trauma patients presenting with systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥ 140 mmHg, administration of tranexamic acid (TXA) does not reduce 28-day or in-hospital mortality and may be associated with an increased risk of thrombotic events compared with patients with lower SBP.

subgroup.split_rule: SBP >= 140 mmHg (first recorded systolic blood pressure on scene or on arrival to ED)
subgroup.notes: Use the first clinically recorded SBP (prehospital if available, otherwise ED triage). If multiple readings exist, use earliest documented value prior to TXA administration. Consider sensitivity analyses using ED-only SBP and prehospital-only SBP. Units = mmHg.

rationale: Physiologic mechanism: TXA inhibits fibrinolysis and shifts the hemostatic balance toward clot preservation. Patients with elevated SBP are less likely to be in hemorrhagic shock and may have lower bleeding burden, so antifibrinolytic therapy could increase thrombotic risk without offsetting reductions in bleeding mortality.

Epidemiologic correlation: Chronic hypertension and elevated presenting SBP are independently associated with higher baseline risk of arterial thrombotic events (MI, ischemic stroke) and microvascular disease, which could increase susceptibility to thrombotic complications when fibrinolysis is suppressed.

Heterogeneous bleeding phenotype: High SBP at presentation often reflects contained hemorrhage, blunt mechanism without massive exsanguination, or preexisting hypertension rather than active severe bleeding; these patients may derive less absolute mortality benefit from hemostatic interventions that primarily prevent exsanguination.

Timing and biology: TXA is most beneficial early in hyperfibrinolytic bleeding states. Elevated SBP may correlate with different pathophysiology (e.g., traumatic brain injury with hypertension or isolated limb injuries) where antifibrinolysis offers limited mortality benefit but could predispose to pathologic thrombosis.

Prior signals and plausibility: While large RCTs (e.g., CRASH-2) show overall benefit in bleeding trauma populations, subgroup analyses are underpowered and there are biologically plausible scenarios where benefit is attenuated or harm emerges—particularly for subgroups with low baseline bleeding risk and higher thrombotic susceptibility.
key_features: First recorded systolic blood pressure (isbp)
History of chronic hypertension or antihypertensive use (if available)
Markers of bleeding severity (e.g., Shock Index, base deficit, hemoglobin, estimated blood loss, transfusion requirement, ISS)
Concurrent antiplatelet/anticoagulant medications
Mechanism of injury and presence of traumatic brain injury (TBI)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by indication and subgroup imbalance: Although TXA assignment is randomized in CRASH-2, this analysis is likely a subgroup (n=200) and randomization may not balance covariates within the SBP-defined strata—leading to residual confounding.

Collider bias: SBP is downstream of both bleeding severity and baseline cardiovascular status. Conditioning on SBP may open colliders between unmeasured factors (e.g., chronic CVD, volume status) and treatment/outcome.

Measurement error and misclassification: Single SBP measurement can be influenced by pain, anxiety, prehospital vasopressors, cuff size, or noisy recording; misclassification around the 140 mmHg threshold may bias estimates toward the null.

Differential timing of treatment: Time from injury to TXA administration modifies TXA effect; if hypertensive patients systematically receive TXA earlier or later, this may confound observed subgroup effects.
Outcome ascertainment and rare events: Thrombotic events are relatively uncommon in trauma datasets and may be under-ascertained, leading to imprecise estimates and false inference about harm.
Sample size and multiplicity: Small subgroup sample (n≈200) yields low power to detect interaction and increases risk of false positives/negatives from multiple post-hoc subgroup tests.

analyses: Descriptive: Compare baseline characteristics (age, sex, ISS, GCS, mechanism, comorbidities, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, time to treatment) between TXA and placebo within the SBP ≥140 and SBP <140 strata to assess balance.

Primary effect-modification test: Fit a multivariable logistic regression for 28-day/in-hospital mortality including main effects for treatment (TXA vs placebo), SBP-group (≥140 vs <140), and their interaction term. Report interaction p-value and subgroup-specific adjusted risk differences and risk ratios with 95% CIs.

Continuous modeling: Model SBP continuously with restricted cubic splines and include an interaction between spline basis and treatment to assess nonlinearity and identify SBP ranges where treatment effect changes.

Stratified causal estimates: Within each SBP stratum, estimate the treatment effect using doubly robust methods (e.g., IPTW with outcome regression or targeted maximum likelihood estimation) adjusting for key confounders (age, ISS, GCS, mechanism, comorbidities, time-to-treatment). Use bootstrap for CIs.

Thrombotic outcomes: Evaluate incidence of clinically adjudicated thrombotic events (MI, ischemic stroke, pulmonary embolism, deep venous thrombosis) within 28 days. Use cause-specific hazard models or Fine-Gray competing risks if bleeding death is a competing event. Report absolute risk differences and number needed to harm if applicable.

Sensitivity analyses: (a) Repeat analyses excluding patients on pre-injury anticoagulants/antiplatelets; (b) vary SBP threshold (e.g., 130, 150 mmHg) and test trend per 10 mmHg; (c) restrict to patients with early treatment (e.g., TXA within 3 hours) to control for timing effect.
Robustness to missing data and measurement error: Perform multiple imputation for missing covariates and compare analyses using earliest prehospital SBP versus ED SBP.
Quantify unmeasured confounding: Compute E-values for observed subgroup effect estimates to assess the minimum strength of unmeasured confounding needed to negate findings.
Reproducibility and meta-analytic check: If possible, pool with other TXA trauma datasets or perform meta-analysis of similar SBP-defined subgroups to assess consistency.
negative_controls: Outcome not plausibly related to TXA (e.g., hospital-acquired urinary tract infection) — expect null effect.
Non-vascular trauma complication with no biologic link to antifibrinolysis (e.g., surgical site infection) as falsification end point.
robustness: Alternate SBP encodings (continuous, quartiles, per-10-mm increment) to check stability of effect.
Use Bayesian hierarchical interaction model to shrink extreme subgroup estimates toward the overall effect, reducing false positives due to small sample size.
Leave-one-hospital or leave-one-site sensitivity to detect influence of clustering or site-specific practice patterns.

caveats: Subgroup inference is not equivalent to causation: Even in randomized trials, post-hoc subgroup analyses are susceptible to chance imbalances and should be interpreted cautiously unless prespecified and replicated.

Power limitations: With ~200 patients, the analysis is likely underpowered to detect modest differences in mortality or rare thrombotic events; wide confidence intervals are expected and lack of statistical significance does not prove absence of effect.

Measurement timing matters: The clinical effect of TXA depends strongly on timing relative to injury; differences in time-to-treatment across SBP strata must be accounted for or may confound interpretation.

Heterogeneity within the subgroup: SBP ≥140 mmHg is a crude marker that mixes acutely hypertensive responses, chronic hypertension, and patients with focal injuries (e.g., TBI) — observed associations may reflect these heterogeneous mechanisms rather than a direct modifying effect of SBP on TXA efficacy.

Outcome ascertainment: Thrombotic events may be underdiagnosed in trauma settings (focus on bleeding/critical care), and coding/ascertainment differences can bias estimates of harm. Confirmatory analyses with adjudicated vascular outcomes or linked administrative data are desirable.

Recommendation for action: Do not change clinical practice solely on this subgroup analysis. Findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require replication in larger datasets, meta-analyses, or mechanistic studies (e.g., fibrinolysis assays) before altering TXA use in hypertensive-presenting trauma patients.

hypotheses.title: Younger trauma patients (<30 years) derive greater mortality benefit from tranexamic acid (TXA)
hypotheses.hypothesis: In trauma patients with significant bleeding or at risk of significant hemorrhage, age < 30 is associated with a larger reduction in 28-day (or in-hospital) all-cause mortality from TXA compared with older patients.

subgroup.notes: iage is numeric age in years. Use strict < 30 as defined; consider sensitivity to inclusive rule (<=30) and alternative cutpoints. Expect fewer events in the subgroup given overall sample size (n=200).

rationale: Physiologic reserve: Younger patients generally have greater cardiovascular and metabolic reserve and fewer chronic comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, diabetes) that can contribute to competing non-hemorrhagic causes of early death; therefore, mortality in younger patients is more likely to be driven by exsanguination and thus more modifiable by an antifibrinolytic such as TXA.

Lower baseline thrombotic risk: Older age is associated with higher baseline thrombotic tendency and more atherosclerotic disease; the net benefit of inhibiting fibrinolysis may be attenuated in older patients if thrombotic complications offset bleeding reduction, whereas younger patients have lower baseline thrombotic risk so the bleeding benefit predominates.

Injury physiology and bleeding patterns: Younger patients often sustain different injury mechanisms (e.g., higher proportion of penetrating or high-energy blunt trauma) and may bleed more rapidly but respond better to hemorrhage control; early inhibition of pathological fibrinolysis (TXA) could therefore have proportionally greater impact on mortality in the younger cohort.

Time-sensitivity of benefit: CRASH-2 and subsequent evidence show TXA benefit is greatest when given early; younger patients may reach care faster or be prioritized differently, so a greater observed benefit could reflect both biology and differential time-to-treatment interacting with age.

Lower competing morbidity and medication effects: Older patients are more likely to be on anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents and have chronic organ dysfunction that alters response to TXA; absence of these modifiers in younger patients increases the likelihood that TXA’s antifibrinolytic effect reduces deaths from bleeding.
key_features: Age (iage) as continuous variable; subgroup defined by iage < 30
Time from injury to treatment (tx_time) — critical effect modifier/confounder
Injury severity (e.g., ISS or proxies such as GCS, systolic BP)
Mechanism of injury (penetrating vs blunt)
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and major comorbidities
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by injury severity: Younger patients may have systematically different ISS, GCS, or physiologic derangement — if not balanced, apparent age-by-treatment effect may reflect severity differences.

Time-to-treatment confounding/interaction: Benefit of TXA is time-dependent; if younger patients receive TXA earlier (or later) than older patients, observed effect modification may be due to treatment timing rather than age per se.
Selection bias/collider bias if subgroup selection conditions on post-randomization variables (e.g., receiving surgery, transfusion volume) that are affected by both age and outcome.

Small-sample and sparse-events bias: Total sample = 200 with likely few deaths in the <30 stratum; effect estimates and interaction tests will be imprecise and unstable (wide CIs, potential for overestimation).

Unmeasured confounding for observational subsets: If analysis uses non-randomized data or deviates from intent-to-treat, baseline differences (comorbidities, prehospital care, anticoagulant use) may bias estimates.
Measurement error or misclassification: Age is usually reliable, but miscoding of other covariates (ISS, mechanism) could distort adjustment and interaction estimates.

analyses: Primary interaction test: fit a logistic regression for 28-day/in-hospital mortality with terms for treatment (TXA vs control), age_group (iage<30), and treatment*age_group interaction. Adjust for pre-specified covariates: ISS (or proxy: GCS, SBP), mechanism (penetrating/blunt), time-to-treatment, anticoagulant use, and center if multi-center. Report interaction OR, 95% CI, and p-value; report absolute risk differences within each age stratum.

Continuous-age analysis: model treatment-by-age interaction using age as a continuous variable (e.g., linear term plus restricted cubic splines) to evaluate non-linear modification and avoid dependence on a single cutpoint. Plot estimated treatment effect (absolute and relative) across age continuum with CIs.

Stratified effect estimates and adjusted causal estimators: within strata (age<30 and >=30) estimate adjusted treatment effect using doubly robust methods (IPTW + regression adjustment) or targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) to obtain marginal risk differences and risk ratios; check covariate balance after weighting.

Time-to-event analysis: fit Cox proportional hazards with treatment, age_group, and interaction, adjusting for covariates; test proportional hazards and report stratified Kaplan–Meier curves and restricted mean survival differences to capture timing of deaths.

Robustness and sensitivity: calculate E-values for observed interaction effect to quantify strength of unmeasured confounding needed to nullify subgroup effect; run sensitivity analyses restricting to patients treated within 3 hours of injury (per CRASH-2 biologic window) and excluding patients on pre-injury anticoagulants.
Multiplicity and power check: compute minimal detectable interaction effect size given n=200 and observed event rates; report post-hoc power or the width of CI to emphasize imprecision.
negative_controls: In-hospital diagnoses unlikely to be affected by TXA (e.g., hospital-acquired urinary tract infection) as a falsification outcome to detect residual confounding or selection bias.
Early non-hemorrhagic causes of death (if separately adjudicated) that would be biologically unlikely to be reduced by TXA.
robustness: Alternative age thresholds (e.g., <25, <35) and continuous spline approach to ensure result not idiosyncratic to chosen cutoff.
Restrict to patients randomized and analyzed by intention-to-treat (if using RCT data) to avoid post-randomization selection bias.
Check balance of key covariates within age strata and after any propensity weighting; if imbalance remains, present both crude and adjusted estimates.
Use bootstrap to assess stability of interaction estimate given small sample and provide percentile CIs for subgroup-specific effects.

caveats: Subgroup interaction does not prove causality beyond the primary randomized comparison — even in an RCT, subgroup tests are often underpowered and susceptible to chance. Findings should be considered hypothesis-generating unless pre-specified and replicated.

Because TXA effect is strongly time-dependent, observed age effect may be mediated or confounded by differences in time-to-treatment; distinguishing mediation from true effect modification is necessary before clinical action.

Small sample (n=200) and likely sparse events in the <30 group substantially increase uncertainty. Negative or positive interaction findings may reflect random variation; report effect sizes with CIs and avoid strong clinical recommendations based on this alone.

If analysis departs from randomized assignment (e.g., per-protocol, observational subset), unmeasured confounding (anticoagulant use, frailty, prehospital care) can produce spurious subgroup effects. Prefer adjusted ITT analyses when possible.

Heterogeneity by age could be secondary to differences in injury mechanism, severity, comorbidity or treatment processes; any observed modification should be checked for these mediators/confounders before attributing effect to biological age.

hypotheses.title: Age ≥ 65: reduced benefit or potential harm from TXA in bleeding trauma patients
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients with significant bleeding or at risk of significant hemorrhage, those aged ≥ 65 years will not derive the mortality benefit from tranexamic acid (TXA) seen in younger patients and may experience increased adverse outcomes (higher 28-day or in-hospital mortality) compared with placebo.

subgroup.notes: Dichotomous split at 65 years. Consider alternate encodings in sensitivity checks (continuous age, age >= 75, and spline-based effect modification). Age measurement in CRASH_2 is expected to be reliable; subgroup size may be small given total N≈200.

rationale: Biologic plausibility: TXA is an antifibrinolytic agent that reduces bleeding but has prothrombotic potential; older adults have higher baseline prevalence of atherosclerotic disease, endothelial dysfunction, and prothrombotic phenotype, which could increase risk of ischemic/thrombotic complications that offset bleeding-related mortality reductions.

Comorbidity burden and competing risks: Elderly trauma patients have higher rates of cardiovascular comorbidity (coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation), baseline anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and frailty; these factors can increase non-hemorrhagic mortality and modify the net effect of TXA.

Heterogeneity of treatment effect in timing and physiology: Benefit of TXA in trauma is time-sensitive (largest when given early); older patients often have delayed presentation/transfer and different injury patterns (e.g., falls), which could reduce the treatment's effective window and thus its benefit while leaving thrombotic risks unchanged.

Prior signals and uncertainty: Some observational data and mechanistic reasoning suggest elevated vascular event risk from prothrombotic therapies in older or frail populations, and randomized-trial subgroup analyses can show attenuated benefit in older strata even if overall trial effect is favorable.
key_features: Age (iage) — dichotomized at 65
Pre-existing cardiovascular disease or vascular risk factors (CAD, PAD, prior stroke)
Pre-injury anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication use
Time-to-treatment (delay from injury to TXA administration)
Markers of injury severity and shock (systolic BP, GCS, transfusion requirement)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by baseline comorbidity: older patients more likely to have cardiovascular disease and be on anticoagulants/antiplatelets, which both alter baseline risk and may interact with TXA effects.
Imbalance within subgroup despite randomization: randomization protects overall but small subgroup sample (N≈200 total) can produce chance imbalances in prognostic covariates within age ≥ 65 stratum.

Selection and collider bias: conditioning on post-randomization variables (e.g., transfusion received, survival to hospital) or on intermediate variables can introduce bias; restricting to survivors to hospital may be a collider.

Measurement/ascertainment differences: older patients may have different patterns of coding for cause of death or adverse events; detection bias for thrombotic events if older patients more intensively monitored for cardiovascular complications.

Effect modification by time-to-treatment and injury mechanism: if older patients systematically receive TXA later or have different injury types (falls vs. high-energy trauma), apparent age effect may be mediated by these variables rather than age per se.

analyses: Estimate subgroup-specific absolute and relative treatment effects (risk difference and risk ratio) for 28-day / in-hospital mortality in age ≥ 65 and age < 65 separately with 95% CIs (use binomial models; present exact counts).

Test for interaction: fit a regression model (log-binomial or Poisson with robust SEs, or Cox PH if time-to-event data available) including treatment, age group, and treatment*age_group interaction; report interaction p-value and interaction estimate (on additive and multiplicative scales).
Continuous-age analysis: model treatment-by-age interaction with age as continuous variable using restricted cubic splines to assess nonlinearity and identify age thresholds where effect changes.

Adjusted doubly-robust estimation: estimate conditional treatment effect in the ≥65 subgroup adjusting for key baseline covariates (injury severity proxies: systolic BP, GCS, mechanism, transfusion need; time-to-treatment; anticoagulant/antiplatelet use; comorbidities) using IPTW or targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) to reduce residual confounding and improve efficiency.

Stratified sensitivity analyses: a) restrict to patients treated within 3 hours of injury; b) exclude patients on pre-injury anticoagulants/antiplatelets; c) stratify by high vs low comorbidity burden (e.g., Charlson index proxy) or frailty proxies to see whether age effect persists after these restrictions.
Precision and power assessment: compute subgroup sample sizes, absolute risk differences detectable with current N, and report wide CIs; avoid binary claims if underpowered.

Unmeasured confounding sensitivity: calculate E-values (or Rosenbaum bounds) for observed subgroup effect estimates to quantify how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away the effect.
Use hierarchical (Bayesian or mixed) models to stabilize subgroup estimates: borrow strength across age groups to avoid extreme estimates driven by small n.
negative_controls: Outcome unlikely to be affected by TXA (e.g., incidence of non-vascular nosocomial infections) to check for residual bias in subgroup selection.
A subgroup not plausibly related to thrombotic risk (e.g., mechanism: penetrating trauma vs blunt) — test for spurious interaction with age to detect analytic artifacts.
robustness: Repeat analyses with alternate age cutpoints (>=75) and continuous-age spline models to ensure findings are not a cutpoint artifact.
Bootstrap CIs for subgroup estimates given small sample size.
Complete-case vs multiple-imputation analyses if covariate missingness exists.
Pre-specify and limit number of subgroup tests or control false discovery (e.g., report all subgroup tests and treat as exploratory).

caveats: Randomized assignment reduces confounding overall, but subgroup analyses (especially with small N) can produce chance imbalances; any subgroup mortality signal should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than definitive evidence of harm.

Observed association between age and reduced benefit or harm may be mediated by correlated factors (time-to-treatment delays, anticoagulant use, injury type, frailty) rather than age per se — careful multivariable adjustment and mediation-aware interpretation are required.

Statistical power is likely limited with total sample ≈200; non-significant interaction does not rule out clinically meaningful heterogeneity, and significant subgroup findings may be imprecise with wide CIs.

Avoid causal language unless interaction is consistently observed across adjusted analyses, sensitivity checks, and is biologically coherent; consider corroboration from larger trials / meta-analysis (e.g., pooled CRASH-2 subgroup data) before changing practice.
Dichotomizing age at 65 is arbitrary and may obscure a continuous relationship; report continuous analyses and alternative thresholds to aid interpretation.

hypotheses.title: Greater mortality benefit from TXA in patients aged <18
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients with significant bleeding or at risk of significant hemorrhage, those aged <18 (pediatric/adolescent) experience greater reduction in 28-day or in-hospital all-cause mortality from tranexamic acid (TXA) than adults (age >=18).

subgroup.notes: Age encoded in years; verify whether age is integer or continuous and how neonates/infants are represented. Consider alternative bins (e.g., <12, 12-17). Confirm that dataset includes accurate weight and dosing information for pediatric patients.

rationale: Biologic plausibility: Younger patients generally have lower baseline thrombotic risk and more preserved hemodynamic and coagulation compensatory mechanisms, so antifibrinolytic therapy (TXA) may reduce hemorrhagic deaths with less offset from thrombotic complications.

Mechanism of trauma coagulopathy: Pediatric physiology can differ from adult trauma-induced coagulopathy; if hyperfibrinolysis is comparatively prominent in children after severe trauma, TXA could produce proportionally greater reductions in bleeding-related mortality.

Lower comorbidity burden: Children/adolescents typically have fewer chronic vascular comorbidities (e.g., atherosclerosis), which could decrease the absolute risk of TXA-associated thrombotic adverse events, improving the net benefit-risk balance.

Temporal window preserved: If pediatric patients are treated early (within the time window where TXA is effective), the relative benefit may be larger because baseline hemorrhagic risk reduction produces a larger proportional effect when competing non-bleeding mortality risks are low.

Empirical signals in literature: Although randomized evidence in pediatrics is limited, observational and mechanistic pediatric trauma data frequently report lower thrombotic complications, supporting a hypothesis of favorable net clinical effect in younger patients.
key_features: iage (age in years) — primary effect modifier
time_to_treatment (minutes/hours) — TXA efficacy highly time-dependent
injury severity (ISS or proxies: GCS, base deficit, systolic BP) — confounder and effect modifier
weight (for pediatric dosing) — potential misclassification if adult dosing applied
mechanism of injury (blunt vs penetrating) and transfusion requirement
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by indication/selection: If TXA administration or inclusion differs by clinician judgment for pediatric vs adult patients (e.g., only the sickest children receive TXA), biased subgroup estimates can result.

Baseline risk differences: Lower absolute mortality in children means measured relative effects can be misleading; small event counts in pediatric stratum increase variability and false-positive risk.
Dose misclassification: Adult-standard TXA regimens may have been used without weight adjustment in children, producing under- or overdosing that modifies effect.

Time-to-treatment / immortal time bias: If children receive TXA earlier or later than adults (or are included only after surviving initial resuscitation), estimates can be biased unless time is correctly handled.

Measurement error and small-sample sparse-data bias: Age misrecording, missing covariates, and few events in the pediatric group can lead to unstable estimates and separation; center-level practices may act as unmeasured confounders (cluster effects).
Generalizability risk: CRASH-2 and many TXA trials primarily enrolled adults; extrapolation to younger ages may be unsupported by randomized pediatric data.

analyses: Descriptive: report counts, event rates, and crude risk difference and risk ratio for 28-day/in-hospital mortality separately for iage < 18 and iage >= 18 with exact (Clopper–Pearson) CIs; report absolute risk reduction (ARR) and number-needed-to-treat (NNT).

Interaction test: fit multivariable model (logistic regression for 28-day mortality or Cox proportional hazards for time-to-death) including treatment, age<18 indicator, and a treatment*age<18 interaction term; report interaction coefficient, 95% CI, and p-value.

Adjusted models: adjust for pre-specified prognostic covariates (injury severity score or proxies: GCS, systolic BP, base deficit/lactate, mechanism of injury, time_to_treatment, transfusion), and include center fixed effects if multicenter. Report stratum-specific adjusted effect estimates (ARR, RR/HR).
Robustness to sparse data: use Firth penalized logistic regression or exact methods if pediatric event counts are low; report bootstrap CIs for ARR and interaction effect.
Propensity-based check: within the non-randomized or imbalanced subset, estimate propensity to receive TXA and perform IPTW or matching, then re-run interaction models to assess consistency.
Time-window sensitivity: repeat analyses restricted to patients treated within the known effective TXA window (e.g., <3 hours) and outside it to assess time-by-age effect modification.

Continuous-age modeling: fit models with age as continuous variable and a continuous treatment-by-age interaction (or spline interaction) to test whether the effect changes smoothly with age rather than at an arbitrary cutoff.

Event-count and power assessment: compute pediatric stratum event counts and minimum detectable interaction size given n=200; if underpowered, present as exploratory and refrain from firm conclusions.
negative_controls: Effect on non-bleeding-specific outcomes (if available), e.g., death from infection or other non-hemorrhagic cause — absence of an effect supports specificity.
Effect on pre-randomization variables (falsification): check that baseline variables measured prior to treatment are not associated with treatment within age strata (sanity check for selection bias).
robustness: Repeat stratified analyses with alternative pediatric cutoffs: <12, <16, and <18 to assess sensitivity to threshold choice.
Multiple imputation for missing covariates and compare complete-case vs imputed results.
Exclude transfers or centers with atypical pediatric practice to assess center-level confounding.
Compute E-values for the observed interaction effect to quantify the strength of unmeasured confounding needed to explain away the interaction (interpret cautiously in RCT vs observational subsets).

caveats: Exploratory subgroup: Unless pre-specified in a trial protocol, subgroup results should be considered hypothesis-generating and not definitive; interaction tests are preferred to separate within-stratum comparisons.
Small pediatric sample and low event counts can produce unstable estimates, wide CIs, and false-positive findings — absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

Causality nuance: even if the parent study is randomized, subgroup analyses can be confounded by post-randomization factors (e.g., differential co-interventions) and should not be overinterpreted as definitive proof of age-specific causal effect modification.

Dosing and physiology differences: pediatric pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics differ from adults and adult dosing may not produce the same exposure — observed differences might reflect dosing rather than true age-based biological effect.

Clinical decision-making: a statistically larger relative effect in children does not automatically translate into practice change unless absolute benefits, safety (thrombotic events), and appropriate dosing are demonstrated in adequately powered pediatric data.

hypotheses.title: Moderate TBI (GCS 9-12) derives greater mortality benefit from tranexamic acid (TXA)
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients with initial Glasgow Coma Scale (igcs) 9–12, administration of tranexamic acid (TXA) reduces 28-day / in-hospital all-cause mortality relative to no TXA, driven primarily by reduced intracranial hemorrhage progression.

subgroup.split_rule: 9 <= igcs <= 12 (restrict analysis to patients whose recorded initial GCS is between 9 and 12 inclusive)
subgroup.notes: Use the first documented pre-hospital or emergency-department total GCS. For intubated patients, document how GCS was scored (e.g., motor-only imputed or reported total). Exclude or flag records with missing/uncertain GCS or imputed values; plan sensitivity analyses for different imputation strategies.

rationale: Mechanistic plausibility: TXA inhibits fibrinolysis and stabilizes forming clots, decreasing hematoma expansion — a major, potentially modifiable mediator of secondary brain injury in patients with intracranial hemorrhage. Patients with moderate TBI (GCS 9–12) are more likely to have salvageable brain tissue where preventing hematoma growth can change outcome, compared with devastating (very low GCS) injuries where primary injury may be irreversible.

Prior trial signal: CRASH-3 and subgroup analyses from related trials reported greater relative benefit of TXA in patients with less severe head injury (mild-to-moderate) than in those with very severe TBI, consistent with a subgroup effect concentrated in GCS >8.

Timing and event rate: Moderate TBI patients have a sufficiently high baseline risk of death driven by hemorrhage progression but also a window for intervention; early TXA (within a few hours) is biologically and clinically more likely to prevent expansion and translate into reduced mortality in this group.

Clinical imaging link: Multiple imaging studies show hematoma expansion in the hours after injury correlates strongly with functional outcome and mortality. Because moderate TBI patients have both a nontrivial rate of hematoma expansion and potential for recovery, preventing expansion is likely to yield measurable mortality reductions.
key_features: igcs (initial total GCS on presentation)
time_from_injury_to_treatment (hours)
presence and size of intracranial hemorrhage on initial CT (if available)
age (older patients have different bleeding risks/outcomes)
baseline physiological severity (systolic BP, pupillary reactivity, ISS)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by indication: clinicians may preferentially give TXA to patients perceived as more likely to bleed or to survive (or conversely to sicker patients), producing biased subgroup estimates if not adjusted.
Measurement error / misclassification of GCS: intubation, sedation, or inconsistent scoring can misclassify patients into the 9–12 window, creating dilution or bias of subgroup effect.
Immortal time and timing bias: if TXA administration time relative to injury differs between groups, earlier-treated patients may appear to benefit due to time-dependent confounding.
Co-interventions and care differences: differential use of neurosurgery, transfusion, reversal of anticoagulation, or critical care resources across groups can confound the observed relationship.
Small sample / sparse events: with total sample size ~200 and only the 9–12 subgroup being smaller, estimates will be imprecise and prone to random fluctuation.

Selection / sampling bias: CRASH-2 (dataset) population and CRASH-3 results differ; applying CRASH-3-derived subgroup expectations to CRASH-2 requires caution because enrollment criteria and case-mix differ.

analyses: Primary test: fit an adjusted logistic regression (or Cox proportional hazards if using time-to-event) for 28-day/in-hospital mortality including terms for treatment (TXA), subgroup indicator (igcs 9–12), and their interaction (TXA * indicator(igcs 9–12)). Report subgroup-specific adjusted odds ratios/HRs, interaction p-value, and absolute risk reduction with 95% CIs.

Doubly-robust estimate within subgroup: within patients with igcs 9–12, estimate treatment effect using targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) or doubly robust AIPW with adjustment set (age, sex, systolic BP, heart rate, time_from_injury, CT bleed, pupillary reactivity, ISS) to obtain adjusted risk difference and relative risk.

Propensity-score analyses: calculate propensity to receive TXA using the same covariates, then (a) perform 1:1 matching or overlap-weighting restricted to the 9–12 subgroup; (b) estimate average treatment effect in the treated (ATT) and average treatment effect (ATE); assess covariate balance after weighting/matching.
Effect modification by time-to-treatment: stratify the subgroup (igcs 9–12) by treatment delay (≤3 hours vs >3 hours) and repeat the above analyses to test whether early TXA drives benefit.

Sensitivity analyses: multiple imputation for missing covariates/GCS; per-protocol excluding patients with protocol deviations or very late TXA; alternative GCS encodings (e.g., motor score alone) to assess robustness to misclassification.

Robustness checks: compute E-value for subgroup effect estimate to quantify unmeasured confounding strength required to negate observed association; bootstrap CIs; Bayesian shrinkage or hierarchical model for subgroup effect to avoid overfitting given small n.
negative_controls: Effect of TXA on an outcome unlikely to be affected by antifibrinolytics (e.g., 28-day rates of hospital-acquired infection) — no association expected.
Effect of TXA on non-head-related causes of early mortality where TXA should not plausibly reduce risk (e.g., deaths attributed to non-bleeding blunt multi-organ failure).
robustness: Repeat analyses restricting to patients with documented intracranial hemorrhage on initial CT to enrich for the mechanism (hematoma expansion).
Exclude intubated/sedated patients or analyze them separately to address GCS misclassification.
Test alternative subgroup boundaries (e.g., 9–13 or 10–12) and report the pattern rather than a single cutpoint to assess sensitivity to chosen threshold.
Use competing-risks analysis (discharge alive) if censoring by discharge is informative.

caveats: Subgroup analyses—even with significant interaction—do not prove causal heterogeneity unless randomization is preserved and sufficiently powered within strata; CRASH-2 is randomized overall, but subgroup estimates can be underpowered and susceptible to chance.

If the analysis is not strictly the original randomized comparison within the subgroup (e.g., excluding patients post-randomization), results may be confounded and should be interpreted as associative rather than causal.

Small sample size and few events in the 9–12 subgroup will yield wide confidence intervals and risk overinterpretation of apparent effects; report effect sizes with uncertainty and consider pooling with external data (e.g., CRASH-3) before changing practice.

GCS is imperfect; misclassification (from sedation/intubation) can bias estimates toward or away from the null. Interpret subgroup patterns in light of sensitivity analyses addressing scoring uncertainty.

Heterogeneity of care (timing of TXA, neurosurgical interventions, imaging availability) may drive observed subgroup differences rather than a true biological interaction—adjustment and stratification for these factors are essential.

hypotheses.title: Severe TBI (GCS ≤ 8) have limited mortality benefit from systemic TXA
hypotheses.hypothesis: In adult trauma patients with severe traumatic brain injury (initial GCS ≤ 8), systemic tranexamic acid (TXA) confers little or no reduction in 28-day / in-hospital all-cause mortality compared with those with higher GCS; the mortality benefit observed in less severe TBI or extracranial bleeding will be attenuated or absent in this subgroup.

subgroup.notes: Use the first documented pre-treatment/ED GCS where available. Flag and account for GCS recorded after intubation/sedation (may require sensitivity analyses or reclassification). If motor/verbal/eye components available, consider motor score-based sub-analyses. Ensure consistent encoding (integer 3-15); treat missingness explicitly.

rationale: Prior randomized-trial evidence (CRASH-3) found the mortality signal for TXA in TBI concentrated in patients with milder injury and within early treatment windows; benefit in isolated severe TBI was uncertain or absent, suggesting effect modification by injury severity.

Pathophysiology: severe primary brain injury (diffuse axonal injury, large primary contusion, brainstem injury) often produces irreversible neuronal damage and rapid fatal herniation, mechanisms that antifibrinolytics cannot reverse even if bleeding expansion is reduced.

In severe TBI, early deaths are frequently driven by primary injury and intracranial hypertension rather than progressive focal hemorrhage; therefore, the potential for TXA to change the dominant causal pathway to death is limited.

Measurement and treatment interactions: severe TBI patients are more likely to be intubated, sedated, receive neurosurgical interventions, and have coagulopathy or multi-organ derangement; these competing interventions and risks can attenuate or obscure the marginal effect of TXA on mortality.

Possible offsetting effects: while TXA could still reduce intracranial hematoma expansion in some severe TBI cases, any small reduction in bleeding-related mortality may be outweighed by irreversible primary injury or by competing complications (e.g., ischemic events), leading to overall minimal net mortality benefit.
key_features: igcs (initial Glasgow Coma Scale score)
pupillary reactivity (unilateral or bilaterally unreactive pupils)
head CT findings (large intracranial hematoma, midline shift, brainstem compression)
time from injury to TXA administration (≤3 h versus >3 h)
presence of major extracranial hemorrhage / hemodynamic instability (SBP)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by severity: GCS both defines subgroup and correlates with many other determinants of mortality (CT lesion type, pupillary response, Injury Severity Score), making residual confounding likely if not fully adjusted.

Measurement error / misclassification: GCS recorded after intubation, sedation, or paralytic administration can under- or over-estimate neurologic injury; inconsistent timing of the GCS measure across subjects can bias subgroup assignment.

Selection and indication bias: clinicians may preferentially give TXA (or withhold it) based on perceived prognosis or presence of extracranial bleeding; in non-randomized settings this will bias effect estimates within subgroups.
Survivor/competing-risk bias: patients with catastrophic brain injury may die before potential benefit from TXA could manifest, producing an apparent lack of effect (competing early mortality).

Treatment interactions and co-interventions: variable use and timing of neurosurgical evacuation, intracranial pressure management, blood products, and reversal of coagulopathy can modify or mask the TXA effect.
Small-sample instability: with n≈200 overall, the severe-TBI subgroup may be small and effect estimates will be imprecise and vulnerable to random imbalances.

analyses: Primary test: fit an adjusted model for 28-day mortality including treatment, GCS<=8 indicator, and a treatment × (GCS<=8) interaction term. Use a generalized linear model for risk ratios (Poisson regression with robust SE) and/or logistic regression; report interaction p-value and subgroup-specific treatment effect estimates with 95% CIs.

Time-to-event: Cox proportional hazards model for time to death (in-hospital or 28-day) including the same interaction term; produce Kaplan–Meier curves stratified by treatment within GCS<=8 and GCS>8 and test for heterogeneity (Wald test on interaction).

Doubly-robust / causal estimation: estimate adjusted average treatment effects within strata (GCS<=8 vs >8) using inverse-probability weighting or targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) adjusting for prespecified confounders (age, sex, systolic BP, RR/oxygenation, time to randomisation/TXA, pupils, major extracranial bleeding, ISS/other markers of injury severity).

Stratified absolute effect: report absolute risk difference and number needed to treat/harm within the severe-TBI subgroup and in the complement; absolute measures are important because baseline risk differs markedly.

Sensitivity analyses: (a) repeat analyses excluding patients with GCS recorded after intubation/sedation or use only pre-hospital GCS where available; (b) stratify by time-to-treatment (≤3 h vs >3 h); (c) vary the GCS cutpoint (e.g., ≤6, ≤9) and treat GCS as continuous with interaction (test for monotonic trend); (d) conduct multiple imputation for missing covariates and compare complete-case vs imputed results.
Robustness to unmeasured confounding: compute E-values for observed subgroup effect estimates to quantify the minimum strength of an unmeasured confounder needed to nullify the observed association.

Assess co-interventions: compare rates and timing of neurosurgical interventions, blood transfusions, and ICP monitoring between treatment arms within the GCS<=8 subgroup to evaluate mediation/interaction.
negative_controls: Test treatment association with outcomes that should be unaffected by TXA (e.g., in-hospital nosocomial infection) as a falsification check for residual confounding.

Use a time-window negative control: evaluate mortality before plausible TXA effect (e.g., death within 30 minutes of arrival) where no treatment effect is expected; a spurious association would indicate bias.
robustness: Propensity-score matching or weighting as an alternative adjustment strategy to check consistency with regression and TMLE estimates.
Exclude early deaths (e.g., within 1–3 hours) to assess influence of immediate catastrophic mortality on effect estimates (competing-risk sensitivity).
Repeat analyses restricted to isolated head injury (no major extracranial hemorrhage) and to patients with confirmed intracranial hemorrhage on CT to evaluate heterogeneity by bleeding source.
Perform influence/leave-one-out analyses if particular centers or extreme cases drive results (use cluster-robust SE for multi-center data).

caveats: Association ≠ causation: subgroup analyses and interaction tests can suggest effect modification but may reflect residual confounding or chance; only randomized assignment within subgroups provides strongest causal evidence.

Power limitations: with roughly 200 patients total, the severe-TBI subgroup may be too small to detect clinically important interaction effects; wide CIs should be anticipated and non-significance does not prove absence of effect.

GCS measurement nuance: GCS is affected by sedation/intubation and by assessor variability; misclassification can bias toward the null or produce spurious interactions—sensitivity analyses using pre-intubation GCS are important.

Heterogeneity within 'severe TBI': GCS ≤8 encompasses diverse pathologies (diffuse axonal injury, large focal hematomas amenable to evacuation); aggregated analysis may obscure subpopulations that do or do not benefit (consider CT-based sub-strata).

Competing interventions and timing: rapid neurosurgical care or late TXA administration (>3 hours) can change the effective treatment contrast; interpretation should account for time-to-treatment and differential co-interventions.

External validity: findings from this CRASH_2-derived sample or HypoGeniC selection may not generalize to other systems with different prehospital care, neurosurgical access, or TXA dosing/timing protocols.

hypotheses.title: Greater benefit of tranexamic acid (TXA) in trauma patients with mild or no TBI (initial GCS >= 13)
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients with initial Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score >= 13, administration of tranexamic acid (TXA) is associated with reduced all-cause 28-day or in-hospital mortality compared with no TXA.

subgroup.split_rule: GCS >= 13 (initial/first-recorded GCS in prehospital or ED assessment)
subgroup.notes: Use first documented GCS after arrival or prehospital assessment. Consider coding GCS missingness explicitly; exclude intubated patients where verbal score missing unless total score reliably recorded. If only component scores present, compute total GCS. If small sample sizes, also report continuous-GCS interaction.

rationale: Mechanistic plausibility: TXA inhibits fibrinolysis and stabilizes formed clots. In patients without severe TBI (GCS >=13), death is more often due to extracranial hemorrhage and exsanguination rather than irreversible brain injury; therefore hemostatic stabilization is more likely to translate into survival benefit.

Evidence from large trauma trials (e.g., CRASH-2) shows TXA reduces death due to bleeding; subgroup and secondary analyses suggest the absolute benefit from hemorrhage control is attenuated when severe TBI is the dominant cause of mortality, implying greater relative/absolute benefit when severe TBI is absent.

Prognostic separation: patients with GCS >=13 are less likely to die from primary neurological injury and have a greater proportion of potentially preventable deaths from hemorrhage or secondary organ failure — mechanisms TXA can modify (reduced transfusion needs, less ongoing bleeding).

Time-to-treatment synergy: early TXA has greatest efficacy for bleeding control. Patients with mild/no TBI are more likely to survive long enough for hemorrhage control interventions to matter, amplifying TXA's effect on preventing exsanguination and subsequent multi-organ dysfunction.

Reduced competing-risk bias: when severe TBI is absent, competing risks from irreversible neurologic death are minimized, increasing the observable effect of an anti-fibrinolytic intervention on all-cause mortality.
key_features: Initial GCS (igcs) — separates severe neurological injury from milder cases
Time to treatment (minutes from injury to TXA administration)
Hemodynamic status (systolic blood pressure, shock index) reflecting bleeding severity
Markers of bleeding/coagulopathy (e.g., base deficit, INR, lactate, transfusion requirement)
Injury mechanism and Injury Severity Score (ISS) — presence of major extracranial hemorrhage
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by indication: clinicians may preferentially give TXA to patients judged more/less likely to survive or those with visible bleeding; this can bias effect estimates unless accounted for.
Measurement error / misclassification of GCS: sedation, intoxication, intubation, or incomplete documentation can misclassify patients into the >=13 subgroup.

Competing risk / collider bias: GCS is both a prognostic marker and possibly influenced by interventions (airway management); conditioning on GCS may introduce collider bias if other factors affect both GCS and TXA receipt.
Immortal time and timing bias: if TXA is given only after a period in which early deaths occur, this can create survivor bias favoring treated patients; time-to-treatment must be considered.
Center/practice heterogeneity: variation in transfusion protocols, surgical control, and critical care across centers may confound observed subgroup effects (cluster effects).
Residual/unmeasured confounding: unrecorded coagulopathy status, prehospital fluids, concomitant hemostatic agents, or differences in injury pattern could explain observed differences.
Small subgroup sample and limited events (sample_size=200) producing imprecise estimates and risk of type I/II errors; overfitting if many covariates are adjusted given few events.

analyses: Descriptive: report counts, baseline characteristics, and crude mortality rates by TXA vs no-TXA within the GCS>=13 subgroup and in the complement (GCS<13). Include absolute risk difference and risk ratio with 95% CI.

Interaction test: fit a model (logistic regression for 28-day/in-hospital mortality or Cox PH if time-to-event available) including main effects for TXA and GCS>=13 and an interaction term TXA * (GCS>=13). Report interaction coefficient, p-value, and subgroup-specific marginal effects.

Adjusted effect estimates: within the GCS>=13 subgroup, estimate treatment effect using multivariable logistic regression adjusting for pre-specified covariates (age, sex, systolic BP, heart rate, ISS or individual injury regions, mechanism of injury, time to treatment, baseline coagulopathy markers, transfusion before/after admission, and center as fixed or random effect). Present adjusted risk difference and odds ratio (or risk ratio via robust Poisson).

Causal/robust estimators: use propensity score methods (IPTW or matching) or doubly robust estimation (targeted maximum likelihood estimation or augmented inverse probability weighting) to adjust for confounding with the same covariates; inspect covariate balance post-weighting/matching.

Timing sensitivity: restrict analyses to patients treated within clinically relevant windows (e.g., TXA within 3 hours of injury) and compare effects; alternatively include time-to-treatment as an interaction or covariate.

Sensitivity to GCS coding: repeat analyses using continuous GCS and alternate thresholds (e.g., >=14) and excluding patients with missing or imputed GCS or those intubated at first assessment to assess robustness to subgroup definition.
Missing data and multiple imputation: handle missing covariates (including igcs if partially missing) with multiple imputation chained equations and compare complete-case vs imputed results.

Cluster and small-sample correction: account for clustering by site (cluster-robust SEs or mixed models) and report exact or penalized logistic regression if events per variable are low to reduce overfitting.
negative_controls: Outcome negative control: an outcome unlikely to be affected by TXA (e.g., hospital-acquired infection rate) — estimate association in the subgroup; a non-null effect suggests residual confounding.
Exposure negative control: examine association of a non-hemostatic medication administered at similar times (if available) with mortality in the same subgroup to detect confounding.
Falsification test: effect of TXA on early non-bleeding death causes (e.g., primary catastrophic brain injury in GCS>=13 subgroup should be minimal).
robustness: E-value calculation to quantify the minimum strength of unmeasured confounding needed to explain away the observed association.
Trim extreme propensity scores and report effect estimates after trimming to assess sensitivity to positivity violations.
Bootstrapped confidence intervals or Bayesian credible intervals for small-sample stability.
Pre-specify and limit number of subgroup and interaction tests; report adjusted p-values or emphasize effect sizes and CIs rather than dichotomous significance.

caveats: Association is not equivalent to causation in observational or post-hoc subgroup analyses; residual confounding and selection bias can produce spurious subgroup effects even after adjustment.

GCS is a strong prognostic marker; a statistical interaction may reflect differences in baseline risk (heterogeneous baseline risk) rather than true modification of TXA's biological effect — examine absolute risk differences and relative effects.

Small sample size (n≈200) and limited events within the GCS>=13 subgroup will yield imprecise estimates; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence and also beware of false-positive findings from sparse data.
Measurement and timing issues: inaccurate or delayed GCS assessment, unrecorded intubation status, and variable time-to-treatment can bias subgroup classification and effect estimates.

External validity: results from the crash_2 dataset (trial or registry subset) may not generalize to different systems of care, prehospital practices, or populations with different baseline risks; where possible, replicate results in larger or randomized datasets.

Harms must also be considered: TXA may increase thrombotic events in some contexts; subgroup benefit on mortality should be weighed against potential harms and secondary outcomes (thromboembolism, seizures).

hypotheses.title: Greater mortality benefit from early TXA in trauma patients with very high initial respiratory rate (irr >= 30/min)
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients with significant bleeding or at risk of significant hemorrhage, those presenting with an initial respiratory rate (irr) >= 30 breaths/min will experience a larger reduction in all-cause 28-day or in-hospital mortality from early tranexamic acid (TXA) administration compared with patients with lower initial respiratory rate.

subgroup.split_rule: initial respiratory rate >= 30 breaths per minute
subgroup.notes: Use first documented respiratory rate on arrival (pre‑intubation if possible). If multiple prehospital/ED values exist, prefer the earliest ED measurement. If intubated before ED measurement, treat as missing or use last pre-intubation value. Consider sensitivity checks using nearby thresholds (e.g., >=28, >=25) and RR recorded within first 15 minutes of arrival.

rationale: Physiologic plausibility: Marked tachypnea (RR >=30/min) commonly reflects significant physiologic stress — hypovolemia, metabolic acidosis, and compensatory hyperventilation — conditions associated with activation of fibrinolysis. TXA inhibits fibrinolysis and therefore may confer greater absolute benefit in patients in whom fibrinolytic activity is heightened.

Severity marker proxy: In settings where blood pressure has not yet collapsed, tachypnea can be an early bedside indicator of severe hemorrhage and high bleeding risk. Prior CRASH-2 analyses showed larger absolute benefit of TXA in higher-risk subgroups (patients more likely to die from bleeding), so a high RR may identify a higher-risk phenotype that stands to gain more from antifibrinolytic therapy.

Temporal plausibility: TXA has the greatest effect when given early. A high initial RR is a rapidly ascertainable sign that may prompt earlier recognition of severe hemorrhage and earlier administration of TXA, making an observable treatment-by-subgroup difference biologically and operationally plausible.

Operational utility: RR is routinely measured at triage and can be used at the bedside without additional tests; if validated, the RR threshold could support rapid treatment decisions in prehospital/ED settings where other markers (lactate, coagulation assays) are unavailable.
key_features: initial respiratory rate (irr)
time from injury to treatment (time-to-TXA)
systolic blood pressure (SBP) — shock index
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) or major TBI indicator (to account for central causes of tachypnea)
heart rate and other physiologic markers of shock (for multivariable adjustment)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Measurement error in respiratory rate: RR is often recorded inaccurately or rounded (e.g., to 20, 30) and may be influenced by agitation, pain, anxiety, or clinician estimation rather than strict counting.

Non-specificity of tachypnea: High RR may reflect traumatic brain injury, chest injury, pulmonary contusion, aspiration, or preexisting pulmonary disease rather than hemorrhagic physiology; these alternate causes could confound observed effect modification.

Differential treatment timing: Patients with very high RR may receive different care pathways (faster TXA, earlier intubation, more rapid transfusion/hemostatic interventions). Because time-to-TXA strongly modifies effect, residual confounding by treatment timing could produce spurious subgroup differences.

Small subgroup counts and low power: With an overall sample size ~200, the number of patients with RR >=30 may be small, producing imprecise estimates and a high risk of chance findings and overfitting.

Post-randomization or collider bias: If subgroup membership is affected by prehospital interventions (e.g., prehospital analgesia, intubation) that themselves relate to outcome, conditioning on observed RR could introduce collider bias. Similarly, restricting analyses to those surviving to get RR measured may introduce selection bias.

Unmeasured confounding: Important covariates (e.g., injury severity score, lactate, transfusion volume) may be unavailable or poorly measured in dataset, leading to residual confounding of subgroup effect estimates.

analyses: Descriptive: report counts, baseline characteristics and crude 28-day/in-hospital mortality rates stratified by subgroup (RR >=30 vs <30) and treatment arm. Present absolute risk differences (ARR) and risk ratios (RR) with exact 95% CIs.

Primary test of interaction (pre-specified): fit an intention-to-treat logistic regression (or Cox model for time-to-event if censoring present) for mortality including terms for treatment, RR30 subgroup indicator, and treatment*RR30 interaction. Adjust for pre-specified covariates: age, sex, systolic BP, heart rate, GCS (or major TBI), time from injury to treatment, mechanism (blunt vs penetrating). Report interaction coefficient, p-value, and interaction-specific effect estimates.

Continuous effect-modification assessment: model initial RR as a continuous variable using restricted cubic splines and include a treatment-by-spline interaction to detect non-linear heterogeneity and avoid arbitrary thresholding. Plot predicted treatment effect (absolute and relative) across RR values with 95% CIs.

Doubly-robust estimation: perform TMLE or augmented IPTW stratified by RR >=30 to estimate average treatment effect within strata, adjusting for the same covariates; compare to unadjusted ITT estimates to assess stability.

Sensitivity analyses: (a) adjust additionally for proxies of bleeding severity if available (pre‑transfusion hemoglobin, transfusion within first 24 h), (b) exclude patients intubated before RR measurement or with major thoracic or CNS injury likely to drive tachypnea, (c) multiple imputation for missing RR and other covariates, (d) test alternative RR thresholds (>=25, >=28) and present results to show threshold sensitivity.

Robustness checks: bootstrap the interaction estimate and construct percentile CIs; perform k-fold cross-validation to assess stability of the subgroup effect discovered by HypoGeniC; report the number of tests performed and adjust for multiplicity or present false discovery rates if multiple subgroups were evaluated.

Falsification/negative controls: test for an interaction between treatment and a baseline variable unlikely to modify TXA effect (e.g., pre-existing chronic conditions not related to bleeding such as diabetes mellitus) and test treatment effect on an outcome unlikely to be affected by TXA (e.g., admission diagnosis of non-bleeding orthopedic injury-related outcomes) to detect residual confounding or data artifacts.

Quantify uncertainty about unmeasured confounding: compute E-values for the observed subgroup-specific treatment effect to characterize the minimum strength of an unmeasured confounder that could explain away the interaction.
