negative_controls: Interaction between TXA and baseline chronic conditions unrelated to bleeding (e.g., diabetes) — expect no effect modification.
Effect of TXA on early non-bleeding outcomes unlikely to be causally affected by antifibrinolytics (e.g., incidence of admission non-hemorrhagic stroke within 24 hours) as a falsification test.
robustness: Check balance of baseline covariates across treatment arms within RR strata — small imbalances may indicate chance imbalance in randomized allocation for the subgroup.
Report subgroup-specific event counts and confidence interval widths; if sparse, present exact methods and avoid overinterpretation.
Repeat analyses excluding patients with likely non-hemorrhagic causes of tachypnea (major TBI, severe chest trauma, pre-existing COPD exacerbation).
Apply multiple thresholds and continuous-spline methods to demonstrate whether the effect is robust to threshold choice and not solely an artifact of cutpoint selection.

caveats: Subgroup findings do not equal proof of causality: even in randomized trials, effect modification analyses are observational within subgroups and are vulnerable to chance imbalances, measurement error, and post-hoc selection; prespecification and replication are required.

Limited sample size: with ~200 patients total, estimates in the RR >=30 group will likely be imprecise; null interaction tests will have low power and positive results may be unstable — report CIs and avoid dichotomous claims.

Measurement limitations: respiratory rate is often error-prone and recorded differently across sites/timepoints; apparent subgroup effects may reflect measurement artifacts rather than true physiology.

Confounding by timing and care: because time-to-TXA and other hemorrhage-directed interventions both influence outcome and may correlate with RR, adjustment and careful sensitivity analyses are essential; residual confounding may still explain observed differences.

Threshold arbitrariness: the chosen cutpoint (>=30/min) is clinically plausible but data-driven selection increases risk of overfitting; present continuous analyses and alternative thresholds to show consistency before recommending clinical uptake.

Need for external validation: any observed effect modification should be validated in larger datasets and pooled individual patient meta-analyses (e.g., full CRASH-2 dataset or other trauma RCTs/cohorts) before changing clinical practice guidance.

hypotheses.title: Limited or no mortality benefit of tranexamic acid (TXA) in trauma patients with low initial respiratory rate (irr <= 12/min)
hypotheses.hypothesis: In trauma patients with significant bleeding or at risk for significant hemorrhage, an initial respiratory rate (irr) <= 12 breaths/min at presentation identifies a subgroup that will derive little or no mortality benefit from tranexamic acid (TXA), compared with patients who present with higher irr.

subgroup.split_rule: <= 12 breaths/min (measured on first clinical assessment prior to airway control/sedation)
subgroup.notes: Use pre-randomization arrival respiratory rate. Exclude RR recorded after intubation, neuromuscular blockade, or heavy prehospital sedation. RR is often rounded (10, 12) and may be missing or imprecise — consider multiple imputation or sensitivity thresholds (<=10, <=14) and continuous modelling with splines.

rationale: Physiologic mechanism: Tachypnea is a common compensatory response to hypovolemia and tissue hypoperfusion. Patients who are not tachypneic (RR <=12) are less likely to have ongoing severe hemorrhage or the degree of physiologic derangement that triggers systemic hyperfibrinolysis; therefore the marginal benefit of an antifibrinolytic drug (TXA) may be smaller in this low-RR group.

Competing-cause mechanism: A low RR at presentation can reflect isolated severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) with respiratory depression or central respiratory compromise. In patients whose mortality is driven primarily by catastrophic brain injury rather than hemorrhage, TXA (targeting bleeding/hyperfibrinolysis) is less likely to reduce all-cause mortality.

Measurement and baseline-risk mechanism: If RR <=12 identifies a subgroup with lower baseline risk of death from exsanguination, then even a constant relative effect of TXA across groups would translate into a smaller absolute mortality benefit in the low-RR group — leading to little or no clinically meaningful benefit.

Confounding/heterogeneity mechanism: Low RR may result from prehospital sedation, alcohol/intoxication, opioid analgesia, or airway compromise. These alternative causes reduce the specificity of RR as a marker for bleeding severity and therefore dilute any true interaction between bleeding physiology and TXA efficacy.
key_features: Initial respiratory rate (irr)
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) or neurologic status (to capture possible TBI-related respiratory depression)
Systolic blood pressure (SBP) and heart rate (HR) as co-physiologic markers of shock
Time from injury to randomization/TXA administration
Intubation / sedation status on arrival
confounders_and_bias_risks: Measurement error and rounding: RR is frequently estimated/rounded (to 10/12), leading to misclassification of the subgroup.
Prehospital/early interventions: Sedation, opioids, alcohol intoxication, or prehospital intubation can lower RR independently of bleeding severity and confound associations.
Severe TBI as competing cause: Low RR may be a marker of severe brain injury which increases mortality through non-hemorrhagic mechanisms (confounding by indication for, or against, TXA).
Residual confounding: Even within an RCT subgroup analysis, baseline imbalance in prognostic covariates across subgroup*arm cells (especially with small N=200) can bias effect estimates.
Collider bias: Conditioning on RR may open backdoor paths if RR is downstream of both unmeasured causes of mortality and bleeding state.
Selection and power issues: Small subgroup sample size increases chance findings and imprecise estimates (wide CIs) and reduces power to detect a true interaction.
Missing data and informative missingness: Missing RR or missing covariates could bias results if not missing at random.

analyses: Primary test: Fit a logistic regression for 28-day/in-hospital mortality including terms for treatment (TXA vs placebo), binary subgroup (irr <=12), and a treatment*subgroup interaction, adjusted for predefined covariates (age, sex, GCS, SBP, HR, mechanism [blunt/penetrating], time to treatment, and site if available). Report interaction p-value, adjusted odds ratios, risk differences and 95% CIs within each stratum.

Continuous modeling: Model RR as a continuous variable (use restricted cubic splines) and include a treatment*spline interaction to assess non-linear effect modification and to visualize treatment effect across the RR range.

Stratified causal estimates: Within irr <=12 and >12 strata, estimate treatment effects using doubly robust methods (e.g., augmented inverse probability weighting or targeted maximum likelihood estimation) adjusted for the same covariates; report absolute risk reduction and number needed to treat with CIs.

Sensitivity exclusions: Repeat analyses excluding patients who were intubated or sedated prior to RR measurement and excluding patients with very low GCS (<9) to reduce TBI-driven mortality confounding.
Threshold and robustness checks: Repeat using alternate thresholds (<=10, <=14) and with multiple imputation for missing RR; perform bootstrapped CIs and examine effect size stability.

Balance checks and PS methods: Within the subgroup strata, check baseline covariate balance by treatment arm; if imbalance present, use propensity score weighting or covariate adjustment to reduce bias.

Power/sample-size assessment: Compute observed subgroup sample sizes and minimum detectable interaction effect (or minimally clinically important absolute risk difference) to contextualize negative findings.
negative_controls: Outcome negative control: hospital-acquired infection (e.g., pneumonia) or other non-bleeding-related outcomes unlikely to be affected by TXA — test for spurious subgroup*tx interactions.
Falsification subgroup: test interaction with a variable unrelated to bleeding physiology (e.g., admission month or non-clinical variable) to check for random subgroup artifacts.
robustness: Multiple imputation for missing RR and covariates; compare complete-case vs imputed results.
E-value calculation for the observed interaction/within-stratum effect estimates to quantify strength of unmeasured confounding required to explain away findings.
Bayesian hierarchical modelling of interaction to borrow strength across RR values and mitigate over-interpretation of noisy subgroup estimates.
Adjust for clustering by enrolling center (random effects) to account for site-level treatment patterns and measurement differences.

caveats: Randomization supports causal estimation of the main TXA effect, but subgroup interaction tests have lower statistical reliability and can be confounded by baseline imbalances — a null interaction does not conclusively prove no differential effect and a positive interaction may be spurious, especially with small N.

A finding of little absolute benefit in the low-RR group could reflect lower baseline risk of bleeding-related death (so absolute benefit is small) while the relative benefit (e.g., relative risk reduction) may be similar to other groups — distinguish absolute vs relative effects in interpretation.

Low RR is a non-specific marker: respiratory depression from TBI, intoxication, or prehospital drugs undermines its specificity for low bleeding severity; therefore any subgroup result must be interpreted in the context of co-variables (GCS, intubation, mechanism).

Measurement imprecision (rounded RR, timing relative to interventions) and small sample size (n=200) limit precision and generalizability; null results should not be taken as definitive evidence to withhold TXA outside a pre-specified, adequately powered interaction analysis.

Multiplicity: multiple subgroup thresholds and post-hoc choices increase false positive risk — pre-specification and replication in independent cohorts or pooled meta-analyses are recommended before changing practice.

hypotheses.title: Moderate tachypnea (initial RR > 18) identifies trauma patients with greater mortality benefit from TXA than normopneic patients
hypotheses.hypothesis: In trauma patients at risk of significant hemorrhage, an initial respiratory rate (irr) > 18 breaths/min defines a subgroup that experiences a greater reduction in 28-day or in-hospital all-cause mortality from tranexamic acid (TXA) compared with patients with irr <= 18 breaths/min.

subgroup.notes: Use the first recorded pre-randomization respiratory rate. Consider treating as a binary split for the primary test but also evaluate RR continuously (splines) and with alternate thresholds (e.g., >16, >20) to assess nonlinearity and threshold sensitivity. Exclude or separately handle cases with missing/implausible RR or patients already intubated at measurement.

rationale: Physiologic marker of bleeding/physiologic stress: Moderate tachypnea (RR >18) commonly reflects increased respiratory drive from hypovolemia, pain, or metabolic acidosis related to ongoing hemorrhage. Patients with physiologic stress from bleeding are more likely to have pathologic fibrinolysis that could be attenuated by TXA, so an increased RR could enrich for those who derive benefit.

Dose–response of physiologic derangement: Trauma interventions (including hemostatic therapies) often show graded benefit with increasing physiologic instability rather than a strict binary threshold; moderate RR elevation may capture an intermediate-risk group with sufficient salvageable risk to demonstrate a measurable, albeit modest, absolute benefit.

RR as an easily measurable triage variable: Respiratory rate is routinely measured pre-hospital and on arrival, making it a pragmatic predictor for early treatment decisions. If modest RR elevation identifies higher absolute benefit, it would have immediate clinical applicability.

Complementary to other vital signs: RR may identify patients with occult bleeding, respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis, or shock states not yet manifest as hypotension; it can therefore detect a population that other single vitals (e.g., systolic BP) miss, potentially enriching the signal for TXA effectiveness.
key_features: Initial respiratory rate (irr)
Time-to-treatment (hours since injury)
Systolic blood pressure (SBP) and heart rate (HR) — markers of shock
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) — injury severity/confounding
Indicator for prehospital or on-arrival intubation / respiratory support
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by severity: Elevated RR correlates with overall injury severity and physiologic derangement (low SBP, tachycardia, low GCS); if not fully adjusted, observed interaction may reflect residual severity differences rather than a true differential treatment effect.

Measurement error and rounding: RR is often measured inaccurately or rounded (e.g., 20), and transient elevations (pain, agitation, anxiety, or prehospital interventions) can misclassify patients into the subgroup.

Collider bias from selection: Restricting analyses to patients who survive long enough to receive TXA or who have complete vitals may induce selection bias; similarly, excluding intubated patients (where RR is unavailable) can induce bias if intubation correlates with both RR and outcome.

Timing confounding: Time from injury to treatment and to RR measurement may differ between subgroups; later treatment generally reduces TXA effectiveness and could confound subgroup effects if moderately tachypneic patients are treated earlier or later on average.
Small-sample instability and multiple testing: With n ≈ 200, subgroup estimates will be imprecise and susceptible to chance findings; data-driven threshold searching increases false-positive risk.

analyses: Primary test: Fit a Cox proportional hazards model (or logistic regression for 28-day mortality if ignoring time) with main terms for treatment (TXA vs control), subgroup (irr > 18), and their interaction. Report interaction p-value, subgroup-specific hazard ratios (HRs) or odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs, and absolute risk differences (ARR) with CIs.

Adjusted models: Repeat the interaction test adding pre-specified confounders: age, sex, SBP, HR, GCS, mechanism of injury (blunt vs penetrating), time from injury to randomization, and center (if multi-center). Use clustered/robust SEs if appropriate.

Continuous modeling and nonlinearity: Model RR continuously with restricted cubic splines and include a treatment-by-RR interaction to assess whether benefit changes smoothly with RR and to identify optimal cutpoints. Visualize predicted treatment effect (ARR or HR) across RR values.

Propensity / causal approaches: Estimate subgroup-specific average treatment effect using propensity-score weighting or doubly robust estimators (IPTW, targeted maximum likelihood estimation) adjusting for baseline covariates. Assess common support and propensity overlap between treatment arms within RR strata.

Sensitivity and threshold checks: Re-run interaction tests using alternative RR thresholds (e.g., >16, >20, >22) and combinations with other vitals (e.g., RR >18 & SBP < 110) to test robustness. Pre-specify thresholds where possible to limit multiplicity.

Timing and per-protocol analyses: Stratify by time-to-treatment (<1 h, 1–3 h, >3 h) and test three-way interaction (treatment × RR subgroup × time) to verify that any subgroup benefit is not explained by earlier treatment. Conduct an as-treated/per-protocol analysis if treatment adherence data exist.

Diagnostics and robustness: Check proportional hazards assumption, estimate E-values for unmeasured confounding, perform multiple-imputation for missing covariates and compare to complete-case results. If sample size allows, bootstrap CIs for subgroup ARR.

Estimate minimum detectable effect: Given the sample size (n~200), compute the minimum detectable interaction effect (or difference in subgroup-specific absolute risks) at alpha=0.05 and power=0.8 to contextualize negative or imprecise findings.
negative_controls: Test for a treatment-by-RR interaction on an outcome unlikely to be affected by TXA (e.g., diagnosis of hospital-acquired non-bleeding infection). A significant interaction would suggest residual confounding or bias.
Use a subgroup defined by a variable unrelated to bleeding physiology (e.g., patient height or laterality of injury) as a falsification test; absence of interaction supports specificity.
robustness: Alternate RR encoding: binary (>18), categorical (≤18, 19–24, ≥25), and continuous splines. Compare conclusions across encodings.
Exclude patients with prehospital or immediate post-arrival intubation or those with missing/implausible RR to evaluate impact of measurement artifacts.
Adjust for additional severity markers (lactate, base deficit, transfusion volume) if available to evaluate residual confounding.
Pre-specify analysis plan and limit post-hoc searching; if multiple thresholds are evaluated, report multiplicity-adjusted p-values or emphasize effect estimates and CIs rather than p-values.

caveats: Association ≠ causation: An observed greater TXA effect in the RR > 18 subgroup would be hypothesis-generating and not definitive proof that RR is an effect modifier; residual confounding or selection bias could produce apparent heterogeneity.
Measurement limitations: RR is prone to inaccuracy and rounding; misclassification will bias interaction estimates toward the null if nondifferential or unpredictably if differential.

Limited power: With ~200 patients, subgroup analyses are underpowered for small/modest differences. Wide CIs are expected; failure to detect an interaction does not rule out clinically meaningful effect modification.
Threshold arbitrariness: The choice of 18 breaths/min is pragmatic but not sacrosanct; results may differ with other cutpoints or when modeling RR continuously.

Clinical heterogeneity: Elevated RR arises from multiple causes (pain, anxiety, pulmonary injury, metabolic acidosis) some unrelated to bleeding. If the subgroup mixes mechanistically distinct patients, any average effect may mask opposing effects in sub-subgroups.

hypotheses.title: Severe intracranial injury (icc >= 3) modifies TXA benefit — lower expected benefit
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients with icc >= 3 (severe intracranial injury), administration of tranexamic acid (TXA) will confer little or no mortality benefit compared with control and will have a lower expected benefit than in patients with icc < 3.

subgroup.notes: icc is the intracranial classification/score available in the crash_2 dataset. Rule uses a binary split at 3 as specified. Consider sensitivity checks using icc as a continuous predictor and alternate cutpoints (e.g., >=4) and cross-tabulation with GCS and CT lesion types to ensure clinical concordance.

rationale: Pathophysiology: In severe intracranial injury (high icc), early mortality is frequently driven by primary brain damage, cerebral herniation, and raised intracranial pressure rather than ongoing systemic haemorrhage; TXA primarily targets fibrinolysis and bleeding, so its ability to reduce mortality is mechanistically limited when non-hemorrhagic irreversible brain injury predominates.

Empirical trial signals: Secondary analyses of large trauma and head-injury trials (for example, CRASH-3 and pooled trauma data) have suggested that the mortality benefit of TXA is largest in patients with less-severe head injury and may attenuate or be absent in those with the most severe head injuries.

Competing risks / limited preventable fraction: Patients with icc >= 3 have a high baseline probability of early death from neurological causes; even if TXA reduces hemorrhagic progression, the absolute risk reduction in all-cause mortality will be smaller because a large fraction of deaths are due to primary brain injury (competing risk).

Time-to-treatment dependence: TXA effectiveness depends on early administration (typically within 3 hours). Patients with severe intracranial injury may die very early or undergo rapid withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies, which reduces opportunity for TXA to impact ultimate mortality.

Potential for harm is uncertain: While major thrombotic harm has not been consistently shown in trials, in severe brain injury any small increase in thrombotic or microvascular complications could theoretically worsen ischemic injury; this supports cautious expectation of little net benefit rather than clear benefit.
key_features: icc (intracranial classification score) — primary subgroup-defining variable
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) — correlates with neurologic severity and may help refine subgroup
Time from injury to randomization / TXA administration — modifier of TXA efficacy
Markers of systemic bleeding/coagulopathy (e.g., systolic blood pressure, base deficit, transfusion requirement) — competing drivers of benefit
Early mortality (e.g., death within 24–48 hours) and decisions to withdraw life-sustaining therapy — influence observed effects
confounders_and_bias_risks: Subgroup-specific imbalance despite randomization: Randomization ensures overall balance, but within the icc >= 3 subgroup (especially with small n ~200) baseline covariates (age, GCS, SBP, comorbidities) may be imbalanced and confound subgroup-specific effect estimates.

Measurement / misclassification of icc: Errors or inconsistencies in assigning icc (imaging timing/quality, inter-rater variability) can dilute differences between subgroups and bias interaction estimates toward the null.

Collider bias from post-randomization care: Subsequent interventions (neurosurgery, intracranial monitoring) or early withdrawal of care may be influenced by both baseline severity and treatment decisions, creating post-randomization colliders if conditioned on in analysis.

Survivor bias / immortal time: Very early deaths before TXA could exert an effect or before reliable icc scoring could be performed may distort apparent treatment effect among those who survive long enough to be scored.

Unmeasured confounding for cause-specific mortality: Cause of death classification errors or unavailable covariates (pre-injury anticoagulant use, CT lesion subtype) can bias interpretation of mechanisms and dilute observable effects on all-cause mortality.

analyses: Primary: Fit an adjusted logistic regression model for 28-day/in-hospital mortality including treatment (TXA vs control), icc>=3 indicator, and a treatment-by-icc>=3 interaction term. Report interaction p-value, subgroup-specific adjusted odds ratios (ORs), absolute risk differences (ARR) and 95% CIs.

Doubly robust estimation: Use propensity score (for icc>=3) weighting or inverse-probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) to estimate marginal treatment effects within the icc>=3 stratum and in the complement, with adjustment for key baseline covariates (age, GCS, SBP, ISS, time to randomization, center).

Time-to-event and competing risks: Estimate cause-specific and subdistribution hazard ratios for time to death (28 days) using Cox models; perform competing-risk analyses separating neurologic (primary brain injury) vs hemorrhagic causes where cause-of-death data are available.
Timing sensitivity: Test effect modification jointly by icc>=3 and time-to-treatment (<1 h, 1–3 h, >3 h). Report whether the attenuation of benefit in icc>=3 is present even for very early treatment.

Robustness / sensitivity: (a) Exclude deaths within 24–48 hours to assess whether very early irreversible deaths drive the null effect; (b) model icc continuously and with alternate cutpoints (>=4), and run E-value or other unmeasured confounding sensitivity analysis to quantify how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away subgroup differences.
negative_controls: Outcome falsification: Test the association of TXA within icc>=3 with an outcome not plausibly affected by TXA (e.g., incidence of non-trauma-related in-hospital infections) to check for residual confounding or systematic bias.

Cause-specific falsification: Evaluate effect of TXA on deaths clearly attributable to non-neurologic causes (if reliably coded) where no effect is expected if the subgroup effect is specific to neurologic competing risks.
robustness: Assess balance of baseline covariates within the icc>=3 subgroup by treatment arm; if imbalanced, present covariate-adjusted and propensity-weighted estimates.
Multiple imputation for missing covariates and sensitivity of results to imputation model; report complete-case and imputed analyses.
Cluster-robust standard errors or random-effects for recruiting center to account for center-level differences in neurosurgical practice and withdrawal-of-care patterns.
Pre-specify and limit the number of subgroup tests; report multiplicity-adjusted inference or present interaction effect sizes with confidence intervals rather than relying on p-values alone.

caveats: Randomization protects against confounding overall, but subgroup estimates (icc >= 3) in small samples (n≈200) have limited precision; a null interaction may reflect low power rather than absence of a true effect.

A reduced or absent mortality benefit in severe intracranial injury does not necessarily imply TXA is harmful — it may simply indicate a smaller absolute preventable fraction of deaths from bleeding in this group.

Interpretation should separate mechanism (TXA effect on haemorrhage progression) from global outcome (all-cause mortality); absence of mortality benefit does not exclude benefit on intermediate outcomes such as hematoma expansion or transfusion reduction.

Post-randomization care decisions (neurosurgery, withdrawal of care) and early deaths can bias subgroup-specific treatment effect estimates; causal claims require careful handling of intermediates and competing risks.

Generalizability: findings from the crash_2 sample and this small subsample may not generalize to other populations, to different definitions of severe intracranial injury, or to settings with different neurosurgical capacity or timing of care.

hypotheses.title: Absence of intracranial injury (icc < 1) identifies trauma patients with greater TXA benefit for extracranial bleeding
hypotheses.hypothesis: In trauma patients enrolled in CRASH_2 with icc < 1 (no or minimal intracranial injury documented), randomised treatment with tranexamic acid (TXA) will produce a larger reduction in 28-day / in-hospital all-cause mortality compared with control than in patients with icc >= 1, because haemorrhage in the icc < 1 subgroup is more likely extracranial and therefore more amenable to systemic antifibrinolytic therapy.

subgroup.split_rule: icc < 1 (patients with no documented intracranial injury)
subgroup.notes: icc should be coded so that 0 = no intracranial injury, 1+ = any intracranial injury. Explicitly treat missing icc as a separate category for sensitivity checks. If icc is ordinal or continuous in the dataset, verify cut-point maps to 'no intracranial injury' and perform continuous modelling as robustness check.

rationale: Mechanistic plausibility: When there is no intracranial injury, fatal outcomes from trauma are more likely driven by extracranial bleeding and exsanguination. TXA inhibits systemic fibrinolysis and reduces bleeding volume and transfusion needs, which should translate into improved survival in extracranial haemorrhage.

Evidence from large RCTs and subgroup considerations: CRASH-2 demonstrated overall mortality benefit from TXA in bleeding trauma; subsequent head-injury–focused analyses (and CRASH-3) suggest that the benefit of TXA depends on the presence and severity of intracranial injury, with little or no benefit in patients whose mortality is overwhelmingly due to primary severe brain injury.

Biomarker/physiology consistency: Patients without intracranial injury are more likely to have treatable bleeding sources (e.g., thoracic/abdominal/pelvic/limb hemorrhage) where systemic antifibrinolysis can reduce ongoing bleeding; conversely, major primary brain lesions may produce early non-bleeding neurological death that is not amenable to TXA.

Observational and subgroup signals: Several observational datasets and pooled subgroup analyses have reported larger effect sizes for TXA in patients without severe head injury or in those with extracranial haemorrhage, supporting the hypothesis that the absence of intracranial injury modifies treatment effect.
key_features: icc (intracranial injury coding) — primary subgroup-defining variable
Time from injury/randomisation to treatment (critical modifier; benefit larger when TXA given early)
Baseline physiology/bleeding severity (e.g., systolic blood pressure, shock index, estimated blood loss, transfusion need)
Injury Severity Score (ISS) or anatomic severity to differentiate death risk from bleeding vs. primary brain injury
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) — complements icc to identify occult brain injury/severity
confounders_and_bias_risks: Residual confounding by baseline bleeding severity: patients with icc < 1 may systematically differ in bleeding load, physiologic reserve, or care received (e.g., faster surgical control) that independently affect mortality and TXA effect estimates.
Measurement error / misclassification of icc: incomplete/immediate imaging, variable documentation, or differing definitions across centres may misclassify patients and dilute subgroup contrast.

Selection and collider bias: restricting to icc < 1 could condition on a collider if factors that influence both the probability of intracranial injury ascertainment and outcome are affected by treatment or other covariates, producing spurious associations.

Differential timing and co-interventions: time to TXA, time to definitive haemorrhage control, transfusion practices, or use of haemostatic agents/surgery may differ between icc strata and confound the apparent effect modification.
Limited sample size (n=200): low power to detect interaction effects and wide CIs; subgroup analyses prone to type II errors and unstable estimates.

Competing risks / cause-of-death heterogeneity: in-hospital all-cause mortality conflates deaths from brain injury, exsanguination, multi-organ failure, and other causes — the mechanism-specific effect of TXA may be masked without cause-specific endpoints.

analyses: Primary test: fit a regression model (logistic regression for 28-day/in-hospital mortality or Cox proportional hazards if time-to-event is available) including main effects for treatment (TXA vs control), icc subgroup (icc < 1 vs icc >= 1), and their interaction term. Report interaction coefficient, p-value, and interaction effect on absolute risk difference scale with 95% CI.

Estimate absolute and relative treatment effects within strata: report risk difference and risk ratio (or hazard ratio) for TXA versus control separately for icc < 1 and icc >= 1, with bootstrap CIs to account for sample-size instability.

Doubly-robust estimation: implement propensity-score–based inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) or targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) within each icc stratum to adjust for key confounders (age, sex, ISS, GCS, systolic BP, HR/shock index, mechanism of injury, time to randomisation, centre) and report marginal effects.

Assess effect modification by time to treatment: repeat interaction analysis stratifying by early treatment windows (e.g., randomisation/treatment within 3 hours vs >3 hours), since TXA efficacy is time-dependent.

Sensitivity analyses for misclassification/missingness: (a) treat missing icc as a separate category and compare results; (b) multiple imputation for missing covariates and icc; (c) model icc continuously or using alternative cut-points (e.g., icc == 0 vs icc >=1) to test threshold robustness.

Power and MDE assessment: compute observed event rates and calculate the minimal detectable interaction (or difference in absolute risk reduction) given n=200 and the observed outcome rates; report that the study may be underpowered for modest interactions.

Falsification / negative-control outcome: test treatment effect on an outcome unlikely to be affected by TXA (e.g., non-bleeding hospital-acquired infection, if recorded) to check for residual confounding or systematic bias.
negative_controls: An outcome unrelated to haemorrhage biology (e.g., hospital-acquired urinary tract infection or other non-bleeding complications) as a falsification test.
A baseline variable measured post-randomisation that should not be affected by treatment (if available) to detect differential measurement or recording bias.
robustness: Repeat analyses with alternative covariate adjustment sets (minimal adjustment: age/sex; clinical adjustment: age, ISS, GCS, SBP; extended adjustment including centre and transfusion volume) to assess stability of interaction estimate.
Use non-parametric or semi-parametric estimators (TMLE or AIPW) to reduce model-dependence.
Exclude early deaths within first few hours (sensitivity to immortal time/measurement bias) and compare results to full-sample analysis.
Perform continuous modelling of icc (if appropriate) and test for non-linear effect modification (e.g., restricted cubic splines) rather than relying solely on a binary cut-point.
Bootstrap-based confidence intervals and permutation testing of the interaction term to account for small-sample distributional issues.

caveats: Although CRASH-2 is a randomized trial (so treatment assignment is unbiased), subgroup analyses (even pre-specified) are inherently less reliable than the overall trial effect; lack of statistical power and multiple testing can produce spurious findings or mask true heterogeneity.

An observed subgroup difference (TXA benefit larger in icc < 1) is effect modification, not proof of mechanism. Demonstrating that extracranial bleeding mediates benefit requires cause-specific death data (bleeding-related mortality) or intermediate outcomes (transfusion volume, rebleeding) which may not be available or complete.

Misclassification of intracranial injury (variable imaging/diagnosis practices) can bias subgroup estimates toward the null or create artifactual interactions; careful variable QC and sensitivity checks are necessary.
Time-to-treatment is a strong effect modifier of TXA efficacy; any subgroup comparison must adjust for or stratify by treatment timing to avoid confounding the icc interaction with delays in care.

With n=200, precision will be limited. Emphasize CIs and effect sizes rather than dichotomous p-value interpretation; consider pooling with external datasets or meta-analytic approaches for more definitive assessment.

If ecological or centre-level differences influence both icc ascertainment and outcomes (e.g., centres with limited CT use may record fewer icc diagnoses and also have different haemorrhage control practices), centre-level confounding should be accounted for (random effects or fixed effects) to avoid biased interaction estimates.

hypotheses.title: Moderate intracranial injury (icc == 2) predicts greater relative benefit from early TXA
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among trauma patients at risk of significant hemorrhage, those with an icc score of 2 (moderate intracranial injury) will experience a larger relative reduction in 28-day or in-hospital all-cause mortality from early tranexamic acid (TXA) than patients with icc == 0 (no intracranial injury) or icc >= 3 (severe intracranial injury), because moderate injury identifies salvageable brain tissue at risk of haemorrhage expansion that TXA can limit.

subgroup.notes: icc is treated as a categorical injury-class variable. Encode missing/icd-unknown as a separate category and consider sensitivity excluding missing. If icc is ordinal 0–3, this rule isolates the middle (moderate) category.

rationale: Pathophysiology: In moderate intracranial injury there is often a substantial volume of brain at risk from expanding intracranial haemorrhage but not yet irreversibly destroyed — a time-limited window when limiting fibrinolysis (with TXA) can reduce haematoma expansion and secondary brain injury.

Clinical trial evidence: CRASH-3 and related analyses reported larger relative reductions in head-injury deaths with early TXA in patients without the most severe head injury compared with those with severe, supporting effect modification by head-injury severity.

Plausible dose–response of salvageability: Patients with no intracranial injury have low head-related mortality and thus limited opportunity for TXA to reduce head-hemorrhage-related deaths; those with severe injury may have irreversible primary brain damage where haemorrhage-limiting therapy yields little mortality gain, making moderate injury the subgroup with the greatest potential absolute and relative benefit.

Timing interaction: TXA efficacy is greatest when administered early (within hours). Moderate injuries are more likely to benefit from early haemostatic intervention because ongoing haemorrhage/expansion continues to drive deterioration in the initial hours after injury.
key_features: icc == 2 (clinical/imaging classification of moderate intracranial injury)
time-to-treatment (early TXA administration)
baseline neurological status / GCS (to adjust for residual severity)
presence/volume of intracranial haemorrhage (if available)
concurrent extracranial bleeding and physiologic instability (BP, shock)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Residual imbalance within subgroups despite randomization: randomization ensures overall balance, but small sample size (n=200) can produce baseline imbalances between treatment arms within icc strata (e.g., age, GCS, SBP).

Confounding by severity and indication: icc==2 patients may differ systematically in other prognostic variables (ISS, extracranial hemorrhage) that affect both mortality and the apparent treatment effect.

Time-to-treatment (immortal time / differential delay): if patients with different icc levels receive TXA at different average times, observed effect modification may reflect timing differences rather than true biological interaction.
Measurement error / misclassification of icc: variability in icc assignment (inter-rater or missing imaging) can attenuate or distort subgroup effects.

Post-randomization interventions (collider bias): differential rates of neurosurgery, transfusion, or ICU care that occur after randomization but differ by icc may introduce bias when conditioning on post-randomization variables.
Small sample and multiple testing: with only ~200 patients, estimates of subgroup interactions will be imprecise and prone to false positives/negatives.

analyses: Primary: Estimate the TXA effect within icc==2 and within comparator strata (icc==0 and icc>=3) separately. Use risk ratios and risk differences for 28-day/in-hospital mortality with 95% CIs. Report absolute and relative measures.

Interaction test: Fit a regression model (preferably a log-binomial or Poisson regression with robust SEs for risk ratios, or Cox model for time-to-death) including treatment, an indicator for icc==2, and a treatment*icc==2 interaction term. Report the interaction coefficient, 95% CI, and p-value.

Covariate-adjusted estimators: Use doubly robust methods (e.g., IPTW or targeted maximum likelihood / augmented inverse probability weighting) to estimate treatment effects within strata and the interaction while adjusting for pre-randomization covariates: age, GCS, systolic BP, heart rate, respiratory rate, ISS or other injury severity measures, time from injury to randomization, and major extracranial bleeding.

Time-to-treatment sensitivity: Restrict analyses to patients randomized/treated within predefined early windows (e.g., <=1 hour, <=3 hours) to assess whether the subgroup effect is dependent on delay.

Ordinal/threshold check: Test for a monotonic trend in treatment effect across ordered icc categories (0,1,2,3) using interaction of treatment with icc as an ordered variable, and compare icc==2 vs icc!=2 contrasts.

Missing data and robustness: Perform multiple imputation for missing covariates/icc and compare complete-case vs imputed results; perform bootstrap CIs for interaction estimates to reflect sample uncertainty.
negative_controls: Outcome not plausibly affected by TXA, for example documented postoperative wound infection or a non-hemorrhagic cause-specific death (if reliably coded) to assess residual bias in subgroup estimates.
A physiologic measure unlikely to be affected by TXA (e.g., admission glucose) as a falsification check for spurious subgroup associations.
robustness: Exclude patients with missing or uncertain icc coding and compare results to the main analysis.
Restrict to patients without major extracranial haemorrhage (or adjust) to reduce confounding by competing sources of bleeding.
Estimate E-values for the observed interaction to quantify how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away the subgroup effect.
Permutation test for the interaction term to evaluate whether the observed interaction is larger than expected by chance given the small sample.
Report both relative (RR, HR) and absolute (risk difference, NNT) measures; absolute measures are less sensitive to baseline risk differences.

caveats: Exploratory subgroup analysis: Even in randomized trials, subgroup interaction tests are observational within subgroups — a statistically significant interaction suggests heterogeneity but does not prove biologic causation without replication.

Limited power: With an overall sample size ~200, tests for interaction will be underpowered; non-significant interaction does not rule out clinically meaningful heterogeneity, and significant interactions may be imprecise.

Generalisability: CRASH-2 is a bleeding-trauma population; prior CRASH-3 head-injury findings support the mechanism but differ in population and design. Any finding here may not directly generalize to pure traumatic brain injury trials.

Outcome attribution: All-cause mortality includes deaths not related to intracranial haemorrhage; an apparent subgroup effect could be diluted or confounded by non-head injury deaths unless cause-specific mortality is examined.

Coding and timing limitations: Misclassification of icc or inaccurate time-to-treatment can bias subgroup effect estimates. Pre-specify rules for handling missing/icc-unknown and for treatment-time windows.

Multiplicity: Multiple subgroup tests increase the false-positive rate. Treat findings as hypothesis-generating and seek replication in larger or pooled datasets (e.g., CRASH-3 or meta-analyses) before changing practice.
